source: Melby-Lervag, Redick, Hulme (2016) Working memory training does not improve performance on measures of intelligence or other measures of far transfer
finding: Meta-analysis of WM training. Near-transfer gains are large. Gains on nonverbal ability (Gf) vanish against active controls.
numbers: 87 publications, 145 comparisons. Nonverbal ability/Gf: active control g=0.05 [-0.02,0.13], k=67; passive control g=0.20 [0.11,0.28], k=53. Near transfer: active g=0.80, passive g=1.88. Verbal WM g=0.31 (active). Visuospatial WM g=0.28 (active).
quote: there is no evidence that working memory training yields improvements in so-called far-transfer abilities.
limits: Immediate posttest mostly. p-curve for active-control studies showed no evidential value (publication bias suspected). Training dose and adult age not reliable moderators. Only first 100k of 235k characters read.
agent_relevance: Raising a capacity measure does not raise reasoning. For an agent, enlarging the working buffer (more context, more rules) cannot be assumed to raise reasoning by itself.

source: Melby-Lervag, Redick, Hulme (2016) mediation and follow-up
finding: Gains on WM measures did not predict gains on Gf, and the nonverbal effect did not persist at follow-up. This is the causal test of the WM-to-Gf link.
numbers: Mediation WM gain -> nonverbal gain: beta=-.01, p=.86, k=26. Follow-up (about 5 months) nonverbal ability, active controls: g=-0.05 [-0.21,0.11], k=12. Verbal WM follow-up g=0.28 [-0.004,0.56], k=10.
limits: A null here does not show the cross-person WM-Gf correlation is non-causal; training may raise task-specific strategy, not the shared capacity.
agent_relevance: Treat WM and reasoning as correlated, not as one lever. Do not expect memory scaffolds to lift reasoning accuracy without testing it.

source: Lawlor-Savage & Goghari (2016) Dual N-Back WM training in healthy adults vs processing-speed training
finding: Five weeks of adaptive dual n-back did not beat an active speed control on WM or Gf in adults aged 30-60. Bayes factors favoured the null.
numbers: 57 analysed (27 WM, 30 PS) of 81. Group x time interaction F(3,52)=0.37, p=.77. Bayes factor for null on Gf interaction 39.97:1. RAPM WM 11.37->11.48, PS 10.56->11.02. Trained n-back level 1.99->3.29.
quote: dual n-back working memory training may not benefit working memory or fluid intelligence in healthy adults
limits: Underpowered by authors own count (139 needed for g=0.24). PS group trained more hours. Home-based Lumosity training. 13-of-25 session cutoff chosen post hoc.
agent_relevance: Failed replication of Jaeggi et al. 2008. Practice on a memory task made people better at the task, not at matrices.

source: Lawlor-Savage & Goghari (2016) literature summary: Au et al. 2014 vs critics
finding: The pro-training meta-analysis (Au et al. 2014) and its critics disagree mainly on control group type.
numbers: Au et al. 2014: 20 studies, N=1,022, g=0.24 for Gf versus controls. Critics (Melby-Lervag & Hulme): active-control estimate about g=0.13. Dougherty et al. 2015 Bayesian reanalysis supported null vs active controls. Redick 2013, Chooi & Thompson 2012, Thompson 2013 found no Gf gain.
limits: Secondhand from a paper that was opened; the original meta-analyses were not opened.
agent_relevance: Even the optimistic estimate (g about 0.13-0.24) is small. Do not budget on a big Gf gain from capacity work.

source: Cochrane, Simmering, Green (2019) Fluid intelligence is related to capacity in memory as well as attention
finding: Gf (Raven) relates to memory tasks and to attention tasks. Attention link to Gf runs fully through WM, but not the reverse. Same pattern in children and adults.
numbers: 42 children (7.1-9.2 y) and 80 adults. Raven r with Spatial Span .412 (adults), .414 (children); N-back .383 / .298. MOT -> Raven mediated by WM composite: direct 0.55 [-0.86,1.97], indirect 9.27 [4.68,13.90]. Reverse path about 50% mediated.
limits: One Gf test, different Raven forms for kids and adults, modest N, correlational. No conventional SEM fit indices. No general positive manifold across all tasks.
agent_relevance: Supports a hierarchy: attention supports the held set, the held set supports reasoning. For an agent, keep the working set small and curated, then reason over it.

source: Cochrane et al. (2019) PCA caution
finding: Exploratory structure was weak. The tasks did not form a clean factor.
numbers: 5 eigenvalues above 1, but only 2 passed parallel analysis (2.96 and 1.44). Enumeration and MOT correlations with Raven not significant in adults (thresholds r=.219 adults, .304 children).
limits: Authors warn against over-reading components. Single-task measures have low reliability.
agent_relevance: Single-task capacity estimates are noisy. Any agent capacity test needs several task variants.

source: Unsworth, Fukuda, Awh, Vogel (2014) Working memory delay activity predicts individual differences in cognitive abilities
finding: Neural delay activity (CDA) predicts Gf, but only via two routes: how many items are held (capacity) and how well attention is controlled.
numbers: N=164 (171 recruited), ages 18-35. CDA with Raven r=-.28 (colour), -.29 (shape). CDA -> gF indirect via capacity -.23; via capacity plus attention control -.41, direct path then not significant. gF model chi2(84)=180.44, RMSEA .08, CFI .93.
limits: Correlational mediation. Low reliability of some tasks (disengagement .22, 48-drop .22). One set size (6) for CDA.
agent_relevance: Capacity alone is not enough. Selecting what to hold (attention control) carries much of the Gf relation. Matches our need for a selection step before storing rules.

source: Robison et al. (2023) Testing locus coeruleus-norepinephrine accounts of WM, attention control, and Gf
finding: Phasic pupil responsiveness (task-evoked) tracks WM capacity, attention control and Gf. Resting-state arousal accounts got no support.
numbers: More than 1,000 participants across 4 studies. Study 1 (N=213) latent r complex span-visual arrays .56; phasic-complex span .21, phasic-visual arrays .38. Study 2 attention control-phasic .68. Four predictors explain 48% of attention-control variance.
quote: Overall, we found no evidence consistent with a resting-state theory.
limits: Pupil is a proxy for LC activity. Studies 3-4 not fully read (page truncated). Many exclusions.
agent_relevance: Effort deployed on the task, not a resting trait, links to reasoning. Analogue: compute spent per item (reasoning effort) matters more than a fixed buffer size.

source: Ruuskanen, Hagen, Espeseth, Mathot (2024) Baseline pupil size seems unrelated to Gf, WM capacity, and attentional control
finding: Failed replication of the claim that resting pupil size indexes WM and intelligence. Bayes factors favour null.
numbers: Groningen N=102, Oslo N=122 (N=224 for Gf). Gf r=-.01, BF01=11.6. WM (N=102) r=.05, BF01=7.26. Attention control r=.11, BF01=4.58.
quote: any relationship between resting-state pupil size and cognitive abilities is likely to be weak or non-existent.
limits: Not preregistered. One task per construct. Attention task split-half only .29. Matrix and WM tasks did not correlate in the sample, which the authors found surprising.
agent_relevance: A reminder that headline WM-intelligence correlates (including physiological ones) fail to replicate at larger N.

source: Kane et al. (2016) Individual differences in the executive control of attention, memory, and thought
finding: WM capacity, attention restraint, attention constraint, mind wandering and RT variability are correlated but separable constructs. WMC links most strongly to restraint (stopping prepotent responses).
numbers: 541 analysed of 545 undergraduates; 472 finished all 3 sessions. 6 WMC tasks, 5 restraint, 5 constraint. Restraint-constraint 95% CI [.46,.74] (not 1.0). WMC-mind wandering about -.20.
limits: No Gf measure in the portion read; only 100k of 294k characters read. Sample oversampled high schizotypy.
agent_relevance: Capacity, inhibition and focus are different levers. A scaffold may need separate guards for each (restrain, constrain, keep on task).

source: Kyllonen & Christal (1990) Reasoning ability is (little more than) working-memory capacity?!
finding: Founding study. Large Air Force samples. Latent WM factor correlated very highly with reasoning factor. Only the title and citation were confirmed (via Wikipedia, Gf page).
numbers: From recall, NOT verified this session: about four studies, N over 2,000 combined, latent correlations roughly .80-.88 (.88 often quoted).
limits: Not opened (paywalled). Numbers unverified. Known issues: overlap in task content and speed demands; Air Force recruits; method variance shared between WM and reasoning tests.
agent_relevance: Origin of the capacity-explains-reasoning claim. Treat the .8-.9 figure as an upper bound that later work reduced.

source: Ackerman, Beier, Boyle (2005) Working memory and intelligence: same or different constructs?
finding: Meta-analysis arguing WM and Gf share limited variance and are different constructs. Reply to Oberauer and Kane et al. followed.
numbers: From recall, NOT verified: about 86 samples; WM-g r about .48; WM-Gf about .36 (uncorrected). Approximate.
limits: Not opened (psycnet did not render). Reanalysed by Oberauer et al. 2005 and Kane et al. 2005 (Psych Bull 131), who argued latent correlations are about .85-.9 once task-specific variance is removed.
agent_relevance: The central dispute: correlation size depends on whether you use single tasks or latent factors.

source: Kane, Hambrick, Conway (2005) WM capacity and fluid intelligence are strongly related constructs: Comment on Ackerman et al.
finding: Rebuttal. Latent-variable studies give much higher WM-Gf correlations than single-task meta-analytic values.
numbers: From recall, NOT verified: reanalysis of 14 datasets, N about 3,000, weighted latent correlation about .72.
limits: Not opened. Numbers unverified.
agent_relevance: Single-benchmark scores underestimate the capacity-reasoning link; use several task variants.

source: Conway, Cowan, Bunting, Therriault, Minkoff (2002) Latent variable analysis of WM, STM, processing speed and Gf
finding: WM capacity predicts Gf; short-term memory and processing speed add little once WM is in the model.
numbers: From recall, NOT verified: N about 120; WM->Gf path about .6.
limits: Not opened (Elsevier blocked). Unverified numbers.
agent_relevance: Storage alone is not the driver; the control component is. Fits the need for active selection.

source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2024) Working Memory Capacity of ChatGPT: An Empirical Study (AAAI-24)
finding: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) shows a human-like n-back capacity limit near n=3. Noise lowers it. Chain-of-thought helps. GPT-4 is far above others.
numbers: Verbal and spatial n-back, n=1,2,3, 50 blocks per cell (30 for model comparison); d-prime falls to about 1 at n=3 in three of four verbal variants. 7 other LLMs (Bloomz-7B, ChatGLM-6B, Vicuna-7B/13B etc.) had very low capacity, nearly identical.
limits: GPT-4 not tested above n=3 (cost). No test of link to reasoning scores.
agent_relevance: A capacity limit appears in LLMs even with full context access. Test n-back style probes on our scaffold, with and without external tracking.

source: Gong et al. (2024) task variants
finding: Grid size, abstract reasoning demands and distractor noise change measured capacity. Larger spatial grids raised capacity (less interference). Abstract reasoning lowered it.
numbers: Spatial variants replicated the decline; CoT significantly improved spatial performance; spatial capacity lower than verbal. Grid sizes 3x3, 4x4, 5x5, 7x7.
limits: No human data for grid size or abstract-reasoning variants (authors say so).
agent_relevance: Interference, not raw slots, sets the limit. Spread rules into distinct, dissimilar items to cut interference.

source: de Langis et al. (2025) Strong Memory, Weak Control: executive functioning in LLMs
finding: LLMs beat human norms on simple and complex spans but fall short on inhibition and flexibility. Bigger WM did not predict better problem-solving. Reasoning models help only partly.
numbers: LLMs perfect up to 50 forward digits, falter at 15 backward digits. Parameter count correlates with mean span r=0.82 (p<.05). Flanker accuracy 40-60% versus human 93-96%. WCST well below human accuracy.
limits: Small model set. Text versions of tasks. Few reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM failure of the Kyllonen-Christal logic: more storage did not give better reasoning. The bottleneck is control (inhibit, shift), which a scaffold can supply.

source: de Langis et al. (2025) reasoning models section
finding: Reasoning (long CoT) models partly compensate: they gain on backward digit span and reading span, but failed to beat non-reasoning counterparts on some control tasks.
numbers: Tested on DeepSeek-R1 distills and a few others; exact per-model gains not extracted.
limits: Only text snippets read, not every table. Directions reliable, magnitudes not captured.
agent_relevance: Written-out tracking turns weak control into usable control. Supports explicit state tracking in the S-states.

source: Xiong et al. (2026) In-context superposition: human-like working memory interference in LLMs (COLM 2026)
finding: LLM n-back accuracy falls with load, is biased by recency, and tracks general capability across models.
numbers: 10 open instruction-tuned models, non-thinking mode, N=1-4. Mean N-back accuracy vs benchmarks (autoregressive): MMLU-Pro r=.78, GPQA Diamond r=.88 (teacher-forced .70/.72), IFEval .69 (tf .82). Log parameter count did not predict the three benchmarks. Qwen3.5 27B beat humans yet still declined with N.
limits: Only 10 models; correlations over few points. Non-thinking mode only. Table significance marks lost in text extraction.
agent_relevance: Best AI analogue of the WM-Gf correlation: LLM n-back correlates with reasoning benchmarks, framed as interference control rather than storage.

source: Xiong et al. (2026) causal intervention
finding: Removing letter-identity directions at the answer position raised n-back accuracy, mostly in weaker models.
numbers: Five LLMs; gains larger in weaker models; stronger models near ceiling. A 2-layer transformer trained on the task solved it perfectly.
limits: Intervention settings selected and evaluated on the same trials (authors say generalisation untested).
agent_relevance: Interference, not slot count, is the target: reduce competing similar items in the prompt.

source: Jaroslawicz et al. (2025) How Many Instructions Can LLMs Follow at Once? (IFScale)
finding: Rule-holding limit for LLMs. Accuracy drops as instructions rise from 10 to 500, with three decay shapes. Best models reach only 68% at 500.
numbers: 20 models, 7 providers, 5 seeds. At 500: o3 62.8%, grok-3 61.9%, claude-3.7-sonnet 52.7%, claude-opus-4 44.6%, claude-sonnet-4 42.9%, deepseek-r1 30.9%, qwen3 26.9%. Reasoning models near-perfect through 100-250 instructions. Floors 7-15% for exponential decayers.
limits: Keyword-inclusion task only, one report format. Not a reasoning measure.
agent_relevance: Direct data on limits on holding many rules. A schema of about 12 guardrails plus a few operators sits well inside the safe range for strong models; weaker models decay early.

source: Jaroslawicz et al. (2025) primacy and error type
finding: Models favour early instructions most at moderate load, then fail uniformly when overwhelmed. Weak models omit instead of attempting.
numbers: Primacy ratio (late/early error) peaks at about 150-200 instructions, converges to 1.0-1.5 above 300. Omission:modification ratio up to 34.88 for llama-4-scout. o3 latency 26s to 220s (10 to 250 instructions).
limits: Same single benchmark.
agent_relevance: Put the highest-priority guardrails first. Reasoning models cost much more time at high density.

source: Patil et al. (2026) Beyond Accuracy: algebraic reasoning failures across nine complexity dimensions
finding: Working memory (parallel independent sub-results) is the dominant scale-invariant bottleneck. All 7 models collapse between 20 and 30 parallel branches.
numbers: 7 instruction-tuned models, 8B to 235B parameters. All score 100% through 12 parallel branches, then collapse at 20-30. GPT-4o Mini step collapse at step 5 in sequential chains. Llama 3 8B fails at 3 ops/branch.
limits: Synthetic algebra only. Models without tools. Hard architectural constraint is the authors interpretation, not tested. Under review at time of posting.
agent_relevance: Cap the number of live partial results in any single step; write intermediates down. About 12 is safe in this task.

source: Wikipedia Working memory (accessed 2026-11-01) summary of training and heritability
finding: Encyclopedia summary: dual n-back effect on Gf reported by Jaeggi 2008, replicated once, then failed in 2012-13; meta-analyses disagree. About half of WM capacity variance is heritable and largely shared with Gf.
numbers: No effect sizes given in the text read. Relational complexity (Halford): performance fell to chance at five interacting variables, read as a limit of about four.
limits: Secondary source; only first 100k of 231k characters read.
agent_relevance: Relational complexity gives a design number: about four variables interacting at once. Keep any single reasoning step near that.

source: Wikipedia Fluid and crystallized intelligence (accessed 2026-11-01) training section
finding: Records Jaeggi 2008 (70 participants, 8-19 days of dual n-back, matrix-test gain) and failures: Chooi & Thompson 2012, Redick et al. 2013, Thompson 2013, with Melby-Lervag & Hulme summary that training effects are short-term and specific.
numbers: Jaeggi 2008: N=70, mean age 25.6, about 25 min/day.
limits: Secondary source. Primary Redick and Jaeggi papers not opened.
agent_relevance: The best-known positive result did not hold; plan for the null.

source: Jaeggi, Buschkuehl, Jonides, Perrig (2008) Improving fluid intelligence with training on working memory
finding: Original dual n-back claim: Gf gain after WM training.
numbers: From the Wikipedia summary only: N=70; Gf gain vs controls; no long-term follow-up. Effect sizes not verified.
limits: Not opened directly. Failed replications: Redick 2013, Chooi & Thompson 2012, Lawlor-Savage 2016 (b03).
agent_relevance: The source of the training claim that did not replicate.

source: Kovacs & Conway (2016) Process overlap theory: a unified account of the general factor of intelligence
finding: Rival theory: the WM-Gf correlation arises from many overlapping processes that tests share, not one capacity.
numbers: From recall, NOT verified: no figures recorded.
limits: Not opened. Other rivals (Cowan focus of attention, Oberauer binding) also unverified here.
agent_relevance: If reasoning is many shared processes, a scaffold should supply several support operations, not one big memory.
